description: We are tech enthusiastic aiming to find our own start up one day.
summary: First Light is a browser game where players design a spacecraft and choose its orbit, then watch a simulation of the mission. When a mission fails, the game explains why, for example a power shortfall, the wrong orbit for the science goal, or running out of fuel. In team mode, each player takes a role (Mission Planner, Science Lead, Engineer or Flight Dynamics) and they design together on their own devices with live sync and conflict alerts, just like a real mission team. Players learn the real trade-offs of mission design by failing safely and trying again.
details:
First Light is a browser game where 1 player, or a team of up to 4, designs a space mission the way NASA teams do, then watches it fly. Your spacecraft dies in its first eclipse. Find out why, fix it, and fly again.

What it does
Players take a mission from idea to “first light”, the moment its first data reaches Earth. They pick a science goal and the instruments that can measure it, set the mission’s priorities, then build the spacecraft: power, battery, computer, pointing, radio and thrusters. They also choose the orbit, rocket and ground stations. Seven resources are checked live: mass, power, budget, data storage, communications, time and delta-v. Every warning is one plain sentence with real numbers and a suggested fix.

The mission then flies in a minute-by-minute simulation. The craft passes through eclipses on battery power, its data piles up between ground passes, its solar panels wear out, drag pulls low orbits down, and random events (a solar storm, a ground station outage, a radio failure) ask the team to decide. The report explains what went wrong, when and why, scores the mission in six categories, and compares it with the last flight. There is rarely one right answer: every mission can be won with several designs.

Four missions: Wildfire Watch (a CubeSat for firefighters, with a tutorial that fails on purpose), Ship Watch (tracking ships at sea), Flood Radar (a radar satellite that sees through storm clouds) and Storm Tracker (a GOES-style weather satellite in geostationary orbit).

How it follows NASA’s process

  • Concept Maturity Levels (JPL): the game’s steps are CML 1 (idea and science goal), CML 2 (feasibility), CML 3 (trade study, which compares two designs) and CML 4 (point design), followed by a design review, launch and flight.
  • The four mission segments from Design and Develop Science Missions are all player decisions: launch, space, ground and user.
  • Mission Design Lab teamwork: each of the four roles (Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, Comms and Flight Dynamics) owns part of the craft, sees only some of the gauges, and has a private goal that pulls against the others. When one player’s change hurts another’s resources, that player is alerted with who did it and why. The whole team moves through the steps together, and 3 stars needs every role’s goal met.
  • Real numbers: parts and rules come from CubeSat 101 and NASA’s State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology. Storm Tracker comes from the NASA GOES-R design overview. Each number names its source in the game, and approximate values are labelled as such.

How we built it
React and TypeScript in the browser, with a 3D spacecraft and launch view in three.js. The game engine (rules, simulation, scoring and report) is plain TypeScript with automated tests, and every number lives in data files that are checked when the game starts. Team play and the leaderboard run on AWS Amplify (AppSync, DynamoDB, Lambda). The leaderboard replays each flight on the server, so scores can’t be faked.

Why it matters
Students rarely get to try a whole mission. First Light lets a beginner (12 and up, no physics needed) design one in about 15 minutes, fail safely, and understand why the trade-offs between mass and power, data and downlink, cost and reliability decide whether a mission succeeds.
dataRefs: CubeSat 101: Basic Concepts and Processes for First-Time CubeSat Developers
